chapter.name: Moving Charges and Magnetism
chapter.blurb: Oersted's discovery that a current deflects a compass needle opens a chapter on how magnetic fields act on moving charges and currents, and how currents in turn produce magnetic fields. It covers the Lorentz force, the force on a current-carrying conductor, circular and helical motion of charges, the Biot-Savart law, the field of a circular loop, Ampere's circuital law for a straight wire and a solenoid, and the force between parallel currents that defines the ampere. It ends with the torque on a current loop, the loop as a magnetic dipole, and the moving coil galvanometer and its conversion into an ammeter and a voltmeter.

scope_in.item: Oersted's observation that a current produces a magnetic field around a wire; the dot (out of the page) and cross (into the page) convention; magnetic fields obey the principle of superposition

Lorentz force F = q[E + v x B]; magnetic force q(v x B): magnitude q v B sin(theta), zero for a charge at rest or moving along the field, perpendicular to v and B, reversed for a negative charge; finding its direction with the right-hand rule (Example 4.2)
Unit of magnetic field: tesla = N s/(C m), defined from F = qvB; gauss = 10^-4 T

Force on a straight current-carrying conductor in an external field, F = I l x B = I l B sin(theta), built from the force on nlA drifting carriers; l along the current, I not a vector; suspension of a wire (Example 4.1), force per unit length in the earth's field (Example 4.9), Exercises 4.5 and 4.6

Magnetic force does no work, so speed and kinetic energy are constant; circular motion for v perpendicular to B with r = mv/(qB), angular frequency qB/m, frequency qB/(2 pi m) and period 2 pi m/(qB) independent of speed (Example 4.3, Exercises 4.11-4.12)
Helical motion when v has a component along B; pitch p = 2 pi m v-parallel/(qB) and radius of the helix

Biot-Savart law dB = (mu0/4 pi) I dl x r/r^3, magnitude (mu0/4 pi) I dl sin(theta)/r^2, direction perpendicular to the plane of dl and r; mu0/4 pi = 10^-7 T m/A; permeability of free space; similarities and differences with Coulomb's law; the relation epsilon0 mu0 = 1/c^2 (Example 4.4)
Applying the Biot-Savart law to elements of straight segments (zero contribution on their own line) and of circular arcs centred on the field point (Example 4.5)

Field on the axis of a circular current loop B = mu0 I R^2/[2(x^2 + R^2)^(3/2)], cancellation of perpendicular components, field at the centre mu0 I/(2R) and mu0 N I/(2R) for N turns; right-hand thumb rule for a loop; closed field lines and north/south faces (Example 4.6, Exercise 4.1)

Ampere's circuital law and its sign convention; Amperian loop and the simplified form B L = mu0 Ie; field of a long straight wire B = mu0 I/(2 pi r), its circular field lines and right-hand rule; field inside and outside a thick wire with uniform current (Example 4.7); law holds for steady currents and is useful only with high symmetry (Exercises 4.2-4.4)

The long solenoid: field inside uniform and parallel to the axis, B = mu0 n I from a rectangular Amperian loop, field outside taken as zero; turns per unit length including multi-layer windings (Example 4.8, Exercise 4.8)

Force per unit length between two long parallel currents f = mu0 Ia Ib/(2 pi d); parallel currents attract, antiparallel repel; equal and opposite forces; definition of the ampere (2 x 10^-7 N/m at 1 m) and of the coulomb; need to eliminate the earth's field; current balance (Exercise 4.7)

Torque on a rectangular current loop in a uniform field: zero net force, torque I A B sin(theta) with theta between the field and the normal; magnetic moment m = N I A with direction from the right-hand thumb rule, tau = m x B, unit A m^2; stable (m parallel to B) and unstable (antiparallel) equilibrium; angular speed gained by a coil turning under the torque (Examples 4.10, 4.11; Exercises 4.9, 4.13)

Circular current loop as a magnetic dipole: far field on the axis (mu0/4 pi) 2m/x^3 and in the plane (mu0/4 pi) m/x^3; analogy with the electric dipole (m with p, mu0 with 1/epsilon0); magnetic monopoles not known to exist

Moving coil galvanometer: radial field and soft iron core, torque N I A B, k phi = N I A B, current sensitivity N A B/k and voltage sensitivity N A B/(k R), effect of doubling the turns; use as a detector with centre zero

Conversion of a galvanometer to an ammeter with a small shunt in parallel (resistance RG rs/(RG + rs)) and to a voltmeter with a large resistance in series; why an ammeter needs a small and a voltmeter a large resistance; effect of the meter's resistance on a simple circuit (Example 4.12, Exercise 4.10)

concepts.name: Magnetic force on a moving charge and the Lorentz force
concepts.description: The force q(v x B) that a magnetic field exerts on a moving charge, its magnitude and direction, the total Lorentz force with an electric field present, and the unit of magnetic field.
concepts.idea: A magnetic field pushes a moving charge sideways, at right angles to both its velocity and the field, and does not act at all on a charge at rest.
concepts.rule: The total force on a charge q moving with velocity v in an electric field E and a magnetic field B is the Lorentz force F = q[E + v x B]. The magnetic part q(v x B) has magnitude q v B sin(theta), where theta is the angle between v and B, so it is zero when the charge is at rest or moves parallel or antiparallel to B, and largest when v is perpendicular to B. Its direction is perpendicular to both v and B, given by the right-hand (screw) rule for v x B, and it is reversed for a negative charge. The SI unit of B is the tesla (T), equal to 1 N s/(C m); a smaller non-SI unit is the gauss, 1 G = 10^-4 T. Magnetic fields from several sources add as vectors (superposition).
concepts.example: With B along +y and a proton moving along +x, v x B is along +z, so the force on the proton is along +z and the force on an electron moving the same way is along -z.

questions.a: The magnitude of the magnetic force is q v B for motion perpendicular to the field. The electron and the proton have charges of the same magnitude e and the same speed in the same field, so the forces are equal in magnitude (e v B). The force is q(v x B), and the charges have opposite signs, so the two forces point in exactly opposite directions.

questions.q: A particle of charge +4 x 10^-6 C moves with a velocity of 3 x 10^3 m/s along the +x axis in a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T directed along the +y axis. Use right-handed axes, for which i x j = k. Find the magnitude and the direction of the magnetic force on it.
questions.a: F = q v B sin(theta) with theta = 90 degrees, so F = 4 x 10^-6 C x 3 x 10^3 m/s x 0.2 T = 2.4 x 10^-3 N. The direction is that of v x B for a positive charge: i x j = k, so the force is along the +z axis.

questions.q: A proton (charge 1.6 x 10^-19 C) moves at 2 x 10^5 m/s along the +x axis through a region where the electric field is 3 x 10^4 N/C along the +z axis and the magnetic field is 0.1 T along the +y axis. Use right-handed axes, for which i x j = k. Find the magnitude and direction of the total (Lorentz) force on the proton.
questions.a: Electric force = qE = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 3 x 10^4 = 4.8 x 10^-15 N along +z. Magnetic force = q v B = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 2 x 10^5 x 0.1 = 3.2 x 10^-15 N, directed along v x B = i x j = k, that is +z. Both forces are along +z, so the Lorentz force F = q[E + v x B] has magnitude 4.8 x 10^-15 + 3.2 x 10^-15 = 8.0 x 10^-15 N along the +z axis.
s: Electric force 4.8 x 10^-15 N and magnetic force 3.2 x 10^-15 N, both along +z

F = q(v x B) = -2 x 10^-6 x (2.0i - 1.5j) x 10^3 = (-4i + 3j) x 10^-3 N. Magnitude = sqrt(4^2 + 3^2) x 10^-3 = 5 x 10^-3 N. Check: F . v is proportional to (-4)(3) + (3)(4) = 0, so F is perpendicular to v, as the magnetic force always is.
s: v x B = (2.0i - 1.5j) x 10^3 evaluated with the correct unit-vector products
F = (-4i + 3j) x 10^-3 N, including the negative sign of the charge
Magnitude 5 x 10^-3 N and F . v = 0 shown

questions.q: Assertion (A): A charged particle moving parallel to a uniform magnetic field experiences no magnetic force. Reason (R): The magnetic force on a charge is q(v x B), and the vector product of two parallel vectors is zero. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: A positive charge moving along the +x axis is found to experience a magnetic force along the +z axis. A student concludes that the magnetic field must point exactly along the +y axis. Use right-handed axes, for which i x j = k. Analyse whether this conclusion necessarily follows.
questions.a: The force q(v x B) is perpendicular to B, so B has no z-component, and i x B = +k requires B to have a positive y-component. But a component of B along the x axis, parallel to the velocity, produces no force at all and so cannot be detected from this one observation. So B lies in the x-y plane with a positive y-component; it need not be exactly along +y.
s: B must have a positive y-component and no z-component
A component of B along v gives no force, so the direction is not uniquely +y

questions.q: Compare the electric force qE and the magnetic force q(v x B) on a charged particle in three respects: (a) dependence on the velocity of the particle, (b) direction of the force relative to the field, and (c) the force on a charge at rest.
questions.a: (a) The electric force qE does not depend on the velocity of the particle, whereas the magnetic force depends on the velocity, being proportional to the speed and to the sine of the angle between v and B. (b) The electric force is along the field E (opposite to E for a negative charge), whereas the magnetic force is perpendicular to the field B and also perpendicular to the velocity. (c) A charge at rest still experiences the electric force qE, but it experiences no magnetic force because v = 0; only a moving charge feels the magnetic force.
s: Velocity dependence compared
Direction relative to the field compared
Charge at rest: electric force acts, magnetic force is zero

questions.q: A student writes: 'A magnetic field has magnitude 1 T if a charge of 1 C moving through it at 1 m/s experiences a force of 1 N, whatever the direction in which the charge moves.' Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is incomplete and, as written, wrong. The magnetic force is q v B sin(theta), so it depends on the angle between v and B; it is zero if the charge moves along the field. The field is 1 T only when the 1 C charge moving at 1 m/s PERPENDICULAR to the field experiences a force of 1 N.
s: Force depends on the angle between v and B (q v B sin theta)
Correct definition requires motion perpendicular to B

questions.q: A uniform magnetic field of unknown magnitude and direction exists in a region where there is no electric field. You have a beam of protons of known speed v and charge e that can be fired in any direction, and you can measure the force on a proton. Design a set of observations that determines both the direction and the magnitude of the field.
questions.a: Step 1: fire the beam in different directions until a direction is found in which the protons experience no force (go undeflected); since the magnetic force vanishes only when v is parallel or antiparallel to B, the field lies along this line. Step 2: fire the beam perpendicular to this line and measure the force F on a proton; since theta = 90 degrees, F = e v B, so B = F/(e v). Step 3: fix the sense of B along the line using the direction of the measured force: for a positive charge the force is along v x B, so of the two possible senses choose the one for which the right-hand rule for v x B gives the observed force direction.
s: Zero-force direction identifies the line of B
Perpendicular firing gives B = F/(ev)
Sense of B fixed from the direction of the force using v x B for a positive charge

concepts.name: Magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor
concepts.description: The force F = I l x B on a straight conductor carrying a steady current in an external uniform magnetic field, built up from the forces on its drifting charge carriers.
concepts.idea: A wire carrying current in a magnetic field is pushed sideways because every drifting charge carrier inside it feels the magnetic force.
concepts.rule: A straight rod of length l and cross-section A with n mobile carriers per unit volume has nlA carriers, each drifting with velocity vd and feeling a force q(vd x B). Adding these gives F = I l x B, where l is a vector of magnitude l along the direction of the current (the current I itself is not a vector) and B is the EXTERNAL field, not the field of the rod's own current. The magnitude is F = I l B sin(theta), where theta is the angle between the conductor and the field: zero when the wire lies along B and largest (I l B) when it is perpendicular. For a wire of arbitrary shape the forces on small straight strips are added.
concepts.example: A wire of mass 200 g and length 1.5 m carrying 2 A stays suspended in mid-air when the upward force I l B balances its weight mg, so B = mg/(Il) = (0.2 x 9.8)/(2 x 1.5) = 0.65 T.

questions.q: A current-carrying wire is electrically neutral as a whole, yet it experiences a force in an external magnetic field. Explain how this force arises.
questions.a: The mobile charge carriers (electrons) in the wire drift with an average drift velocity vd when a current flows, so each one experiences a magnetic force q(vd x B); the fixed positive ions are at rest and feel no magnetic force. Adding the forces on all nlA drifting carriers in a length l gives (nlA) q vd x B = I l x B, which is the force on the wire.
s: Drifting carriers each feel q(vd x B); stationary ions feel none
Sum over nlA carriers gives F = I l x B

questions.q: A straight wire of mass 60 g and length 0.5 m is to be suspended in mid-air by a uniform horizontal magnetic field of 0.4 T that is perpendicular to the wire. Take g = 10 m/s^2. Find the current needed in the wire.

I = 3 A

questions.q: A straight wire 4.0 cm long carrying a current of 5 A is placed inside a long solenoid where the magnetic field is 0.30 T along the solenoid's axis. Find the magnetic force on the wire when it is held (a) perpendicular to the axis and (b) parallel to the axis.
questions.a: (a) Perpendicular to the axis the wire is perpendicular to B, so F = I l B = 5 A x 0.040 m x 0.30 T = 0.06 N. (b) Parallel to the axis the wire lies along B, so sin(theta) = 0 and the force is zero.

(b) F = 0 since the wire is along the field

questions.q: A horizontal rod carrying a current hangs from two identical vertical springs in a uniform horizontal magnetic field that is perpendicular to the rod. With the current in one direction the springs stretch more than with no current; with the current reversed they stretch less. Explain these observations.
questions.a: The magnetic force I l x B on the rod is perpendicular to both the rod and the horizontal field, so it is vertical. For one direction of current it points downward and adds to the weight, so the springs stretch more. Reversing the current reverses l and hence the force, which now points upward and partly balances the weight, so the springs stretch less.
s: Force I l x B is vertical; downward for one current direction, adding to the weight
Reversing the current reverses the force to upward, reducing the stretch

questions.q: A long straight wire of mass per unit length 0.02 kg/m carries a current of 5 A towards the east and is to be held suspended in mid-air by a uniform horizontal magnetic field. Take g = 10 m/s^2. (a) Find the smallest field that can do this and its orientation relative to the wire. (b) State, with reasoning, whether this field must point north or south. (c) If instead the horizontal field makes an angle of 30 degrees with the wire (sin 30 = 0.5), find the field magnitude now needed.
questions.a: (a) Per unit length, I B sin(theta) = (m/l) g. The field needed is smallest when sin(theta) = 1, that is when B is perpendicular to the wire: B = (m/l) g / I = (0.02 x 10)/5 = 0.04 T. (b) The force I l x B must point upward. With the current towards the east, east x north = up, so the field must point towards the north (a field towards the south would give a downward force). (c) Now I B sin 30 = (m/l) g, so B = 0.04/0.5 = 0.08 T.
s: (a) B = 0.04 T, perpendicular to the wire
(b) Field towards north, since east x north = up

questions.q: A student writes the magnetic force on a straight conductor of length vector l carrying current I in a field B as F = I (B x l). Evaluate whether this is acceptable.
questions.a: It is not acceptable. The force is F = I (l x B), and a vector product reverses sign when the order of its factors is exchanged, so B x l = -(l x B). The student's expression gives the correct magnitude I l B sin(theta) but exactly the opposite direction.
s: Correct order is l x B; exchanging the order reverses the vector
Magnitude would be right but the direction is opposite

questions.q: Design an experiment that uses a straight horizontal rod carrying a known current, resting on a sensitive electronic balance, to measure the magnitude of an unknown uniform horizontal magnetic field between the poles of a magnet. State what is measured and how the field is calculated.
questions.a: Place the rod on the balance so that a known length l of it lies horizontally between the poles, perpendicular to the horizontal field, with flexible leads so the connections exert no force. With no current, note the balance reading. Pass a known current I: the vertical magnetic force I l B changes the reading by an amount delta-m (in kg), so I l B = (delta-m) g and B = (delta-m) g/(I l). Reverse the current to check that the change in reading reverses sign, and repeat for several currents; a graph of (delta-m) g against I is a straight line of slope l B, from which B is found.
s: Arrangement: rod of known length perpendicular to the horizontal field, on a balance
Measurement: change in balance reading for a known current, I l B = (delta-m) g
B = (delta-m) g/(I l), with a check by reversing or varying the current

concepts.name: Motion of a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field
concepts.description: Circular motion when the velocity is perpendicular to B (radius, angular frequency, period) and helical motion with a pitch when the velocity also has a component along B.
concepts.idea: Because the magnetic force is always at right angles to the velocity, it changes only the direction of motion: the particle goes round in a circle, or along a helix if it also moves along the field.
concepts.rule: The magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and the speed and kinetic energy stay constant. If v is perpendicular to a uniform B, the force q v B acts as the centripetal force: m v^2/r = q v B, giving radius r = m v/(q B). The angular frequency is omega = q B/m, the frequency is q B/(2 pi m) and the period is T = 2 pi m/(q B), all independent of the speed and energy. If the velocity also has a component v-parallel along B, that component is unchanged and the path is a helix; the distance moved along the field in one rotation is the pitch p = v-parallel x T = 2 pi m v-parallel/(q B), and the radius of the circular part is the radius of the helix.
concepts.example: An electron (mass 9 x 10^-31 kg, charge 1.6 x 10^-19 C) moving at 3 x 10^7 m/s perpendicular to a field of 6 x 10^-4 T moves in a circle of radius r = mv/(qB) = 28 cm.

questions.q: For a charged particle moving along a helical path in a uniform magnetic field, the distance moved along the field in one rotation is called the ____ of the helix (one word).
questions.a: pitch

questions.q: A charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field with its velocity exactly perpendicular to the field. No other force acts. Its path is
questions.a: a circle in a plane perpendicular to the field
o: a circle in a plane perpendicular to the field
a straight line along the field

The electric force qE can have a component parallel or antiparallel to the motion, so it can do work on the particle and change its kinetic energy.

Period is independent of speed

(b) T = 2 pi m/(q B) = 2 x 3.14 x 1.6 x 10^-27/(1.6 x 10^-19 x 0.1) = 6.28 x 10^-7 s. (c) Pitch p = v-parallel x T = 1.0 x 10^5 x 6.28 x 10^-7 = 6.28 x 10^-2 m = 6.28 cm.

questions.q: Design a method, using a uniform magnetic field of known magnitude B, to find the ratio of charge to mass (q/m) of an unknown charged particle and the sign of its charge. State what you would measure and how the result is calculated.

Measure the radius r of the circle (for example from the diameter between the point of entry and the point where the particle returns after half a circle). Since m v^2/r = q v B, the ratio is q/m = v/(r B). Alternatively measure the frequency of revolution f and use q/m = 2 pi f/B, which needs no knowledge of the speed. The sign of the charge follows from the sense of rotation: the force on a positive charge is along v x B, so a positive particle bends one way and a negative particle the opposite way in the same field.
s: Arrangement: velocity perpendicular to known B, circular path
Measure r (with known v) and use q/m = v/(rB), or measure frequency and use q/m = 2 pi f/B
Sign of charge from the sense of deflection, using v x B

concepts.name: Biot-Savart law for a current element
concepts.description: The magnetic field dB produced by a small current element I dl at a point: its dependence on current, length, angle and distance, its direction, and its comparison with Coulomb's law.
concepts.idea: Each tiny piece of a current-carrying wire produces its own small magnetic field, which circles around the piece and gets weaker as the square of the distance.
concepts.rule: For an element dl of a conductor carrying current I, the field at a point with displacement vector r from the element is dB = (mu0/4 pi) I (dl x r)/r^3, with magnitude dB = (mu0/4 pi) I dl sin(theta)/r^2, where theta is the angle between dl and r and mu0/4 pi = 10^-7 T m/A (mu0 is the permeability of free space). The direction of dB is perpendicular to the plane containing dl and r, given by the right-hand screw rule for dl x r. The field is zero at points along the line of the element (theta = 0) and largest, for a given distance, at theta = 90 degrees. Like Coulomb's law it is an inverse-square, long-range law obeying superposition, but its source I dl is a vector, its field is perpendicular to r rather than along it, and it depends on angle. The total field is found by adding (integrating) dB over the whole conductor.
concepts.example: An element of length 1 cm along +x at the origin carrying 10 A gives, at a point 0.5 m away on the y axis, dB = 10^-7 x 10 x 10^-2/(0.5)^2 = 4 x 10^-8 T, directed along +z since i x j = k.

questions.q: The constant mu0 that appears in the Biot-Savart law is called the ____ of free space (one word).

questions.q: According to the Biot-Savart law, the magnitude of the magnetic field due to a small current element, at a point at distance r from it in a fixed direction, is proportional to

(3) The Biot-Savart law has an angle dependence (sin theta), so the field is zero along the line of the element, whereas the field of a point charge has no such angle dependence.

A current element of length 2 cm lies at the origin along the +x axis and carries a current of 8 A in the +x direction. Take mu0/(4 pi) = 10^-7 T m/A. Use right-handed axes, for which i x j = k. Find the magnitude and direction of its magnetic field at the point on the y axis with y = +0.4 m.
questions.a: dB = (mu0/4 pi) I dl sin(theta)/r^2 with theta = 90 degrees: dB = 10^-7 x 8 x 0.02/(0.4)^2 = 1.6 x 10^-8/0.16 = 1.0 x 10^-7 T. The direction is that of dl x r, that is i x j = k, so the field is along the +z axis.
s: Direction +z from dl x r

questions.q: A current element of length 1 mm lies at the origin and carries a current of 25 A in the +x direction. Take mu0/(4 pi) = 10^-7 T m/A. Use right-handed axes, for which i x j = k. Find the magnitude and direction of its magnetic field at the point P with coordinates (0.3 m, 0.4 m, 0).
questions.a: The distance is r = sqrt(0.3^2 + 0.4^2) = 0.5 m, and the angle theta between the element (along x) and r has sin(theta) = 0.4/0.5 = 0.8. dB = 10^-7 x 25 x 10^-3 x 0.8/(0.5)^2 = 2 x 10^-9/0.25 = 8 x 10^-9 T. Direction: i x (0.3i + 0.4j) = 0.4k, so the field is along the +z axis.
s: r = 0.5 m and sin(theta) = 0.8 used to get dB = 8 x 10^-9 T
Direction +z

questions.q: A long wire lying in the plane of the page carries a current of 10 A. In the middle it is bent into a semicircular arc of radius 5 cm, and the two straight portions lie along one straight line that passes through the centre O of the arc. The current goes round the arc clockwise as seen by the reader. Applying the Biot-Savart law directly to the current elements, find the magnitude and direction of the magnetic field at O. Take mu0/(4 pi) = 10^-7 T m/A. Take pi = 3.14.
questions.a: Straight portions: every element dl is parallel (or antiparallel) to the displacement r from it to O, so dl x r = 0 and they contribute nothing. Arc: every element is perpendicular to r and at the same distance R, and all the contributions dB = (mu0/4 pi) I dl/R^2 point the same way, so they add: B = (mu0/4 pi) I (pi R)/R^2 = (mu0/4 pi) pi I/R. B = 10^-7 x 3.14 x 10/0.05 = 6.28 x 10^-5 T. Direction: for a clockwise current, dl x r points into the page, so the field at O is perpendicular to the page and directed into it.
s: Straight portions contribute zero because dl is parallel to r
Arc: B = (mu0/4 pi) pi I/R = 6.28 x 10^-5 T
Direction into the page

questions.q: Consider these statements. (I) The magnetic field of a current element at a point is directed along the line joining the element to that point. questions.a: Only II

questions.q: A small current element produces a field at two points. Point P is at distance r from the element in the direction perpendicular to it. Point Q is at distance r/2 in a direction making 30 degrees with the element (sin 30 = 0.5). At which point is the field larger, and by what factor?
questions.a: dB is proportional to sin(theta)/r^2. At P: sin 90/r^2 = 1/r^2. At Q: sin 30/(r/2)^2 = 0.5 x 4/r^2 = 2/r^2. So the field is larger at Q, and it is 2 times the field at P.
s: dB proportional to sin(theta)/r^2 applied to both points
Field at Q is twice the field at P

questions.q: A wire carrying a current of 8 A consists of a quarter-circle arc (one-fourth of a circle) of radius 0.1 m with centre O, joined at each end to a straight wire that runs along a radius, directly away from O. Using the Biot-Savart law, analyse the contribution of each part and find the magnitude of the magnetic field at O. Take mu0/(4 pi) = 10^-7 T m/A. Take pi = 3.14.
questions.a: Radial straight wires: each element dl lies along the line through O, so dl is parallel or antiparallel to r, dl x r = 0, and they contribute nothing at O. Arc: each element is perpendicular to r and at distance R, and all contributions are in the same direction (perpendicular to the plane of the arc), so B = (mu0/4 pi) I (arc length)/R^2 with arc length = (2 pi R)/4 = pi R/2. Hence B = (mu0/4 pi) pi I/(2R) = 10^-7 x 3.14 x 8/(2 x 0.1) = 1.256 x 10^-5 T, about 1.26 x 10^-5 T, which is one-fourth of the field a complete circle of the same radius and current would give at its centre.
s: Radial wires contribute zero (dl parallel to r)
Arc contributions all add: B = (mu0/4 pi) I (pi R/2)/R^2

questions.q: A student says: 'Since the Biot-Savart law is an inverse-square law like Coulomb's law, a current element produces a field of the same magnitude at all points that are at the same distance from it.' Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is wrong. The Biot-Savart field also depends on the angle theta between the element and the line to the point, through the factor sin(theta). At the same distance the field is largest in directions perpendicular to the element and falls to zero at points along the line of the element, unlike the field of a point charge, which is the same in all directions at a given distance.
s: Field depends on sin(theta), not on distance alone
Maximum perpendicular to the element, zero along its line

questions.q: Create a numerical problem of your own in which a small current element placed at the origin produces a magnetic field of magnitude exactly 2 x 10^-8 T directed along the -y axis at a chosen point, and solve it to show that your numbers work. Take mu0/(4 pi) = 10^-7 T m/A. Use right-handed axes, for which i x j = k.
questions.a: One possible problem: an element of length 1 cm at the origin carries 5 A in the +z direction; find its field at the point x = -0.5 m on the x axis. Solution: the point is in a direction perpendicular to the element, so dB = (mu0/4 pi) I dl/r^2 = 10^-7 x 5 x 0.01/(0.5)^2 = 5 x 10^-9/0.25 = 2 x 10^-8 T. Direction: dl x r is along k x (-i) = -j, so the field is along the -y axis, as required. (Any consistent choice with I dl sin(theta)/r^2 = 0.2 A/m and dl x r along -y earns full credit.)
s: A complete, self-consistent problem stated (current, length, direction, point)
Magnitude worked out to 2 x 10^-8 T
Direction shown to be -y using dl x r

concepts.name: Magnetic field on the axis of a circular current loop
concepts.description: The field of a circular loop or coil at a point on its axis and at its centre, obtained by adding the Biot-Savart contributions of its elements, with its direction given by the right-hand thumb rule.
concepts.idea: Every bit of a circular current loop pushes the field at the centre the same way along the axis, so a loop acts like a short magnet with a north face and a south face.
concepts.rule: For a circular loop of radius R carrying a steady current I, the field at a point on the axis at distance x from the centre is B = mu0 I R^2/[2 (x^2 + R^2)^(3/2)], directed along the axis. Each element gives dB = (mu0/4 pi) I dl/(x^2 + R^2); the components perpendicular to the axis cancel in pairs from diametrically opposite elements and only the axial components dB cos(theta), with cos(theta) = R/(x^2 + R^2)^(1/2), add up. At the centre (x = 0) the field is B = mu0 I/(2R), and for a tightly wound coil of N turns it is N times as large. Direction: curl the fingers of the right hand round the loop in the direction of the current; the thumb gives the direction of the field. The field lines are closed loops, and the face of the loop from which they emerge behaves like a north pole.
concepts.example: A tightly wound coil of 100 turns and radius 10 cm carrying 1 A has a field at its centre of B = mu0 N I/(2R) = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 100 x 1)/(2 x 0.1) = 6.28 x 10^-4 T.

questions.q: Two concentric circular loops lie in the plane of the page. Direction along the axis, from the coil towards the observer at P

questions.q: Two identical single-turn circular loops, each of radius 3 cm and each carrying 5 A, are placed with a common axis, their centres 8 cm apart. Point M is the midpoint between the centres, on the axis. Take mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A. Analyse the field at M (a) when the currents go round in the same sense and (b) when they go round in opposite senses. Give magnitudes in terms of pi.
questions.a: M is 4 cm from the centre of each loop, so for each loop x^2 + R^2 = 16 + 9 = 25 cm^2 = 25 x 10^-4 m^2 and (x^2 + R^2)^(3/2) = (0.05)^3 = 1.25 x 10^-4 m^3. Field of one loop at M: B = mu0 I R^2/[2 (x^2 + R^2)^(3/2)] = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 5 x 9 x 10^-4)/(2 x 1.25 x 10^-4) = 7.2 pi x 10^-6 T along the axis. (a) Same sense: by the right-hand thumb rule both fields point the same way along the axis, so they add: 1.44 pi x 10^-5 T (about 4.5 x 10^-5 T). (b) Opposite senses: the two fields at M are equal and opposite, so the net field at M is zero.
s: Field of one loop at M = 7.2 pi x 10^-6 T
(a) Same sense: fields add to 1.44 pi x 10^-5 T
(b) Opposite senses: net field zero

questions.q: A wire is bent into a semicircular arc. A student claims: 'Each element of the semicircle is at the same distance from the centre as in a complete circle of the same radius, so the semicircle gives the same field at the centre as the complete circular loop carrying the same current.' Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. It is true that every element is at the same distance from the centre and that all contributions point the same way, but the total field is the sum over all the elements, and a semicircle has only half the length of current-carrying wire that a full circle has. So the field at the centre due to the semicircular arc is half that of the complete loop, with the direction still given by the right-hand rule.
s: Field is the sum over all elements; a semicircle has half the length
So the field is half that of the full loop

questions.q: Design a tightly wound circular coil that produces a magnetic field of 1.0 x 10^-3 T at its centre using a current of not more than 2 A. Take mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A. Take pi = 3.14. State the number of turns, the radius and the current you choose, and verify your design by calculation.
questions.a: One possible design: N = 100 turns, radius R = 6.28 cm = 0.0628 m, current I = 1 A (within the 2 A limit). Check: B = mu0 N I/(2R) = (4 x 3.14 x 10^-7 x 100 x 1)/(2 x 0.0628) = (1.256 x 10^-4)/(0.1256) = 1.0 x 10^-3 T, as required. (Any choice with N I/R = 1.0 x 10^-3 x 2/(4 pi x 10^-7), about 1592 A/m, and I not exceeding 2 A earns full credit.)
s: Uses B = mu0 N I/(2R) to set the requirement on N, I and R
States a definite design with I not more than 2 A
Verifies numerically that B = 1.0 x 10^-3 T

concepts.name: Ampere's circuital law: the long straight wire and the solenoid
concepts.description: Ampere's circuital law and its use, with a suitable Amperian loop, to find the field of a long straight wire (outside and inside the wire) and of a long solenoid.
concepts.idea: Going once round any closed path, the total of 'field along the path times length' depends only on how much current threads through the path.
concepts.rule: Ampere's circuital law: the line integral of B.dl round a closed loop equals mu0 times the total current I passing through the surface bounded by the loop, with the sign of the current fixed by the right-hand rule (fingers along the sense of traversal, thumb along positive current). When B is tangential and constant over a length L of an Amperian loop (and normal to the loop or zero elsewhere), this becomes B L = mu0 Ie, where Ie is the enclosed current. For a long straight wire, B x 2 pi r = mu0 I gives B = mu0 I/(2 pi r) outside the wire; the field lines are circles concentric with the wire, with direction given by the right-hand rule (thumb along the current, fingers curl along B). Inside a wire of radius a with uniformly distributed current, the enclosed current is I r^2/a^2 and B = mu0 I r/(2 pi a^2), so B is proportional to r inside and to 1/r outside. For a long solenoid with n turns per unit length carrying current I, the field inside is uniform, parallel to the axis and equal to B = mu0 n I, and the field outside is taken as zero. The law holds for steady currents and is useful only in situations of high symmetry.
concepts.example: A solenoid 0.5 m long with 500 turns has n = 1000 turns/m; carrying 5 A, the field inside is B = mu0 n I = 4 pi x 10^-7 x 1000 x 5 = 6.28 x 10^-3 T.

questions.q: In the expression for the magnetic field inside a long solenoid, n stands for the number of turns per unit ____ of the solenoid (one word).
questions.a: length

questions.q: Ampere's circuital law states that the line integral of the magnetic field B round a closed loop is equal to
questions.a: mu0 times the total current passing through the surface bounded by the loop
o: mu0 times the total current passing through the surface bounded by the loop
the total current passing through the surface bounded by the loop divided by mu0
mu0 times the total charge enclosed by the loop

questions.q: A long straight wire carries a steady current I. The magnitude of the magnetic field at a distance r from the wire (outside it) is
questions.a: mu0 I/(2 pi r)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about an ideal long solenoid carrying a steady current is NOT correct?
questions.a: The field inside is strongest on the axis and falls steadily towards the windings
o: The field inside is strongest on the axis and falls steadily towards the windings
The field inside is parallel to the axis of the solenoid
The field outside the solenoid is taken to be zero
The field inside is proportional to the number of turns per unit length

questions.q: A long straight wire carries a steady current. The magnetic field at a point 2 cm from the wire is ____ times the field at a point 6 cm from the wire (a whole number).
The magnetic field lines due to a long straight current-carrying wire are
questions.a: circles concentric with the wire, in planes perpendicular to it
o: circles concentric with the wire, in planes perpendicular to it
straight lines parallel to the wire
straight lines pointing radially away from the wire

questions.q: A long straight vertical wire carries a current vertically upward. At a point due east of the wire, the magnetic field due to the wire is directed towards the
questions.a: north

questions.q: A long straight wire of circular cross-section of radius a carries a steady current distributed uniformly over its cross-section. As the distance r from the axis of the wire increases from zero, the magnitude of the magnetic field
questions.a: increases in proportion to r up to r = a and then falls as 1/r
o: increases in proportion to r up to r = a and then falls as 1/r
is zero up to r = a and then falls as 1/r
is constant up to r = a and then falls as 1/r
falls as 1/r for all values of r

questions.q: A rectangular Amperian loop abcd is drawn for a very long solenoid, with side ab of length h inside the solenoid along its axis and side cd outside. Explain how Ampere's circuital law leads to the field inside the solenoid, where n is the number of turns per unit length and I the current.
questions.a: Along cd the field is zero, since the field outside a long solenoid is taken as zero. Along the transverse sides bc and da the field has no component along the sides, so they contribute nothing. Only ab contributes, giving B h for the loop. The number of turns passing through the loop is n h, so the enclosed current is n h I. Ampere's law gives B h = mu0 n h I, so B = mu0 n I.
s: Only the inside side ab contributes (B h); outside and transverse sides give zero
Enclosed current n h I, hence B = mu0 n I

questions.q: A long straight wire carries a current of 30 A. Take mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A. The magnitude of the magnetic field at a point 15 cm from the wire is
A long solenoid of length 0.4 m has 800 turns and carries a current of 2 A. Take mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A. The magnitude of the magnetic field inside the solenoid is
A horizontal overhead power line carries a current of 60 A from west to east. Take mu0/(4 pi) = 10^-7 T m/A. The magnetic field due to this current at a point 1.5 m directly below the line is
questions.a: 8 x 10^-6 T, towards the north

questions.q: A long straight wire of circular cross-section of radius 2 mm carries a current of 10 A distributed uniformly over its cross-section. Take mu0/(4 pi) = 10^-7 T m/A. Use Ampere's circuital law to find the magnitude of the magnetic field at a point inside the wire, 1 mm from its axis.
questions.a: Take a circular Amperian loop of radius r = 1 mm concentric with the wire. The enclosed current is Ie = I r^2/a^2 = 10 x (1/2)^2 = 2.5 A. Ampere's law: B x 2 pi r = mu0 Ie, so B = (mu0/2 pi) Ie/r = 2 x 10^-7 x 2.5/(1 x 10^-3) = 5 x 10^-4 T.
s: Enclosed current Ie = I r^2/a^2 = 2.5 A
B = mu0 Ie/(2 pi r) = 5 x 10^-4 T

questions.q: A closely wound long solenoid 50 cm long has 4 layers of windings of 250 turns each and carries a current of 5 A. Take mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A. Find, in terms of pi, the magnitude of the magnetic field inside the solenoid near its centre.
questions.a: Total turns N = 4 x 250 = 1000, so n = N/length = 1000/0.5 = 2000 turns/m. B = mu0 n I = 4 pi x 10^-7 x 2000 x 5 = 4 pi x 10^-3 T (about 1.26 x 10^-2 T).
s: n = 2000 turns per metre, counting all layers
B = mu0 n I = 4 pi x 10^-3 T

questions.q: Two long straight parallel wires P and Q are perpendicular to the plane of the page and cut it at two points 10 cm apart, with P on the left and Q on the right. P carries 6 A out of the page and Q carries 4 A into the page. Take mu0/(4 pi) = 10^-7 T m/A. Find the magnitude and direction of the net magnetic field at the point midway between them.
questions.a: The midpoint is 0.05 m from each wire. B due to P = (mu0/2 pi) I/r = 2 x 10^-7 x 6/0.05 = 2.4 x 10^-5 T. B due to Q = 2 x 10^-7 x 4/0.05 = 1.6 x 10^-5 T. Directions by the right-hand rule: for P (current out of the page) the field lines run anticlockwise, so at the midpoint, to the right of P, the field points towards the top of the page. For Q (current into the page) the field lines run clockwise, so at the midpoint, to the left of Q, the field also points towards the top of the page. The fields add: B = 2.4 x 10^-5 + 1.6 x 10^-5 = 4.0 x 10^-5 T, directed in the plane of the page towards the top of the page (perpendicular to the line joining the wires).
s: Individual fields 2.4 x 10^-5 T and 1.6 x 10^-5 T
Both point the same way at the midpoint (right-hand rule)
Net field 4.0 x 10^-5 T towards the top of the page

questions.q: Consider these statements. (I) The magnetic field of a long straight current-carrying wire has the same magnitude at every point of a circle that is centred on the wire and lies in a plane perpendicular to it. (II) Ampere's circuital law, as used for finding magnetic fields, holds for steady currents that do not change with time. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Both I and II

questions.q: Ampere's circuital law holds for any closed loop. Explain why it nevertheless gives the field of a long straight wire easily, but cannot conveniently be used to obtain the field at the centre of a circular current loop.
questions.a: To extract B from the law one needs an Amperian loop along which B is tangential and constant in magnitude (or else normal to the loop or zero). The long straight wire has cylindrical symmetry, so on a concentric circle B is tangential and the same everywhere, and the law gives B x 2 pi r = mu0 I at once. The circular current loop has no such symmetry: no simple closed path through its centre has B constant and tangential along it, so although the law is still true, B cannot be taken out of the integral and the field has to be found from the Biot-Savart law.
s: Need a loop on which B is tangential and constant; the straight wire's symmetry provides it
No such loop exists for the field at the centre of a circular loop, so the law is true but not useful there

questions.q: A long straight wire of circular cross-section of radius a carries a steady current I distributed uniformly across the cross-section. Using Ampere's circuital law, obtain the magnitude of the magnetic field (a) at a distance r greater than a and (b) at a distance r less than a from the axis, and (c) show that the two results agree at the surface and state where the field is greatest.
questions.a: (a) For r > a take a circular Amperian loop of radius r concentric with the wire; it encloses the whole current, so B x 2 pi r = mu0 I and B = mu0 I/(2 pi r), which falls as 1/r. (b) For r < a the loop encloses only the fraction of current in area pi r^2: Ie = I (pi r^2)/(pi a^2) = I r^2/a^2. Then B x 2 pi r = mu0 I r^2/a^2, so B = mu0 I r/(2 pi a^2), which increases in proportion to r. (c) At r = a both expressions give B = mu0 I/(2 pi a), so they agree. Since B rises with r inside and falls with r outside, the field is greatest at the surface of the wire, r = a.
s: (a) B = mu0 I/(2 pi r) for r > a
(b) Ie = I r^2/a^2 and B = mu0 I r/(2 pi a^2) for r < a
(c) Both give mu0 I/(2 pi a) at r = a; field is greatest at the surface

questions.q: A student calculates the field at the centre of a coil of length 4 cm and radius 3 cm by using the result for a long solenoid. Evaluate whether this is a sound thing to do.
questions.a: It is not sound. The long-solenoid result assumes that the solenoid's length is large compared with its radius, so that the field inside is uniform and parallel to the axis and the field outside is negligible. Here the length (4 cm) is comparable with the radius (3 cm), so these assumptions fail: the field is not uniform, the outside field is not negligible, and the long-solenoid result would not give the correct value.
s: Long-solenoid result needs length much greater than radius
Here length is comparable to radius, so the result is not reliable

questions.q: Design a long solenoid that produces a magnetic field of 2 pi x 10^-3 T inside it using a current of not more than 5 A. Take mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A. State the length, the radius, the total number of turns and the current you choose, verify the field by calculation, and say why your solenoid can be treated as 'long'.
questions.a: Requirement: B = mu0 n I, so n I = (2 pi x 10^-3)/(4 pi x 10^-7) = 5000 A/m. One possible design: current I = 2.5 A and n = 2000 turns per metre, obtained by winding 1000 turns uniformly over a length of 0.5 m, on a former of radius 1 cm. Check: B = 4 pi x 10^-7 x 2000 x 2.5 = 2 pi x 10^-3 T, as required, and 2.5 A is within the limit. The length (50 cm) is 50 times the radius (1 cm), so the solenoid is long and the result B = mu0 n I applies near its middle.
s: Requirement n I = 5000 A/m obtained from B = mu0 n I
A definite design (length, turns, current not above 5 A) verified numerically
Length much greater than radius justified

concepts.name: Force between two parallel currents and the definition of the ampere
concepts.description: The magnetic force per unit length between two long parallel current-carrying conductors, its direction (attraction or repulsion), and how it was used to define the ampere and the coulomb.
concepts.idea: Each wire sits in the magnetic field of the other, so two current-carrying wires push or pull on each other: currents the same way pull together, currents opposite ways push apart.
concepts.rule: Conductor a carrying current Ia produces at conductor b, a distance d away, a field Ba = mu0 Ia/(2 pi d). Conductor b, carrying Ib, then experiences a force Ib L Ba on a length L, so the force per unit length is f = mu0 Ia Ib/(2 pi d). The force on a due to b is equal and opposite (consistent with Newton's third law). Parallel currents attract and antiparallel currents repel - the opposite of the rule for electric charges. This force was used to define the ampere: it is that steady current which, maintained in each of two very long, straight, parallel conductors of negligible cross-section placed one metre apart in vacuum, produces on each a force of 2 x 10^-7 newton per metre of length. The coulomb is then the charge that flows through a cross-section in 1 s when the steady current is 1 A.
concepts.example: Two long parallel wires 0.1 m apart carrying 5 A and 10 A exert on each other a force per unit length f = mu0 Ia Ib/(2 pi d) = 2 x 10^-7 x 5 x 10/0.1 = 1 x 10^-4 N/m.

questions.q: In the definition of the ampere, the two very long, straight, parallel conductors are placed ____ metre apart in vacuum (a whole number).
Two long straight parallel wires carry steady currents in the same direction. The magnetic forces between them make the wires
questions.a: attract each other
o: exert no force on each other
twist about each other without attracting or repelling

Which of the following statements about the magnetic forces between two long straight parallel current-carrying wires is FALSE?
questions.a: The wire carrying the larger current exerts the larger force on the other wire
o: The wire carrying the larger current exerts the larger force on the other wire
Wires carrying currents in opposite directions repel each other
The force per unit length becomes smaller when the wires are moved farther apart
The force on a wire is proportional to the length of that wire considered

Two long parallel wires carry steady currents. If the current in only one of the wires is tripled, with everything else unchanged, the force per unit length on each wire
questions.a: becomes three times as large
o: stays the same on the other wire and triples on this one

questions.q: The rule for the force between two parallel currents, compared with the rule for the force between two electric charges, is that
questions.a: like (parallel) currents attract, whereas like charges repel
o: like (parallel) currents attract, whereas like charges repel
like (parallel) currents repel, just as like charges repel
like (parallel) currents attract, just as like charges attract
parallel currents exert no force, whereas like charges repel

questions.q: Two long straight horizontal wires run east-west, with wire A directly above wire B. Both carry current towards the east. The magnetic force on wire A due to wire B is directed
questions.a: vertically downward

questions.q: Explain, in two stages, how a long straight wire a carrying a current exerts a force on a parallel wire b carrying a current in the same direction, and why this force is an attraction.
questions.a: Stage 1: the current in wire a produces a magnetic field at the position of wire b; this field is the same at all points along b and is perpendicular to b (by the right-hand rule, circling round a). Stage 2: wire b carries a current in this external field, so it experiences a force I l x B, which is perpendicular to both b and the field, that is, along the line joining the wires. Working out the direction of l x B for currents in the same direction shows that this force is directed towards wire a, so the wires attract.
s: Wire a produces a field at b, perpendicular to b
Wire b carrying current in this field feels I l x B, directed towards a (attraction)

questions.q: Two long straight parallel wires 0.1 m apart carry currents of 5 A and 10 A. Take mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A. The magnitude of the force per unit length on each wire is
Two long straight parallel wires 4 cm apart each carry a current of 2 A, in opposite directions. Take mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A. The force on a 0.5 m length of either wire is
questions.a: 1 x 10^-5 N, repulsive

questions.q: Two long straight parallel wires A and B, 3 cm apart, carry currents of 6 A and 5 A respectively in the same direction. Take mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A. The force on a 20 cm section of wire A is
questions.a: 4 x 10^-5 N, towards B

questions.q: Two long straight parallel wires 2 cm apart carry equal currents and repel each other with a force of 1 x 10^-3 N per metre of length. Take mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A. Find the current in each wire and state the relative directions of the two currents.
questions.a: f = mu0 I^2/(2 pi d) = 2 x 10^-7 x I^2/d. So I^2 = f d/(2 x 10^-7) = (1 x 10^-3 x 0.02)/(2 x 10^-7) = 100, giving I = 10 A in each wire. Since the wires repel, the currents are in opposite directions (antiparallel).
s: Currents are in opposite directions because the force is repulsive

questions.q: Two long straight parallel wires P and Q, 5 cm apart, carry currents of 4 A and 6 A in the same direction. Take mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A. Find the force on a 1 m length of P and on a 1 m length of Q, stating the direction of each.
questions.a: f = mu0 Ia Ib/(2 pi d) = 2 x 10^-7 x 4 x 6/0.05 = 9.6 x 10^-5 N/m. So the force on 1 m of P is 9.6 x 10^-5 N directed towards Q, and the force on 1 m of Q is 9.6 x 10^-5 N directed towards P: the forces are equal and opposite, and the wires attract because the currents are parallel.
s: Force 9.6 x 10^-5 N on each metre
Equal and opposite, each directed towards the other wire (attraction)

questions.q: A long straight wire A is fixed horizontally and carries a current of 50 A. A second long wire B, carrying 20 A, is to float freely in the air, parallel to A and 1 cm vertically above it, supported only by the magnetic force from A. Take mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A. Take g = 10 m/s^2. (a) State, with a reason, whether the current in B must be in the same direction as that in A or opposite to it. (b) Find the mass per unit length of wire B.
questions.a: (a) B is above A and needs an upward force, that is, a force directed away from A - a repulsion. Antiparallel currents repel, so the current in B must be opposite in direction to that in A. (b) Force per unit length f = mu0 Ia Ib/(2 pi d) = 2 x 10^-7 x 50 x 20/0.01 = 2 x 10^-2 N/m. For B to float, f = (mass per unit length) x g, so mass per unit length = (2 x 10^-2)/10 = 2 x 10^-3 kg/m (2 g per metre).
s: (a) Currents opposite, because repulsion is needed to give an upward force
Mass per unit length = f/g = 2 x 10^-3 kg/m

questions.q: Assertion (A): Two long straight parallel wires carrying steady currents in opposite directions attract each other. Reason (R): The magnetic forces that two long parallel current-carrying wires exert on each other are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, R is true
o: A is false, R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false

questions.q: Three long straight parallel wires A, B and C lie in one plane, with B midway between A and C; the spacing between neighbouring wires is 10 cm. Each wire carries 10 A in the same direction. Take mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A. Find the net force per unit length (a) on B and (b) on A, with direction.
questions.a: (a) B is attracted towards A and towards C by equal forces per unit length, 2 x 10^-7 x 10 x 10/0.1 = 2 x 10^-4 N/m each, in opposite directions, so the net force on B is zero. (b) A is attracted towards B with 2 x 10^-4 N/m and towards C (0.2 m away) with 2 x 10^-7 x 100/0.2 = 1 x 10^-4 N/m. Both forces point the same way, so the net force per unit length on A is 3 x 10^-4 N/m, directed towards B (and C).
s: (a) Net force on B is zero (equal and opposite attractions)
(b) Net force on A = 3 x 10^-4 N/m towards B

questions.q: At a certain place the horizontal component of the earth's magnetic field is 3.0 x 10^-5 T. A long straight wire carrying 1 A lies horizontally, perpendicular to this component. (a) Find the force per unit length on the wire due to the earth's field. (b) Compare it with the force per unit length that appears in the definition of the ampere. (c) Hence explain what must be done in practice when the ampere is standardised.
questions.a: (a) f = I B sin 90 = 1 x 3.0 x 10^-5 = 3.0 x 10^-5 N/m. (b) The definition of the ampere involves a force of 2 x 10^-7 N per metre between two wires carrying 1 A each, 1 m apart. The force due to the earth's field is (3.0 x 10^-5)/(2 x 10^-7) = 150 times larger. (c) So the effect of the earth's magnetic field (and other stray fields) must be eliminated when the ampere is standardised; in practice the very long wires are also replaced by multi-turn coils of suitable geometry, and the mechanical force is measured with an instrument called the current balance.
s: (b) Definition force 2 x 10^-7 N/m; earth's effect is 150 times larger
(c) Earth's field and stray fields must be eliminated (multi-turn coils, current balance)

questions.q: A student says: 'The force on wire b due to a parallel wire a depends only on the current in wire a, because it is wire a that produces the magnetic field.' Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is wrong. Wire a's current does fix the field Ba at wire b, but the force on wire b is the force on a current-carrying conductor in that field, Ib L Ba, which is proportional to wire b's own current as well. So the force on b is proportional to the product of the two currents; if b carried no current it would feel no force.
s: Field at b depends on Ia, but force on b = Ib L Ba
Hence force depends on the product of both currents

questions.q: Design a simple current balance that could be used to measure a steady current by means of the force between two parallel conductors carrying that same current. Describe the arrangement, what is measured, how the current is calculated, and one precaution.
questions.a: Arrangement: two long straight parallel conductors of length L, a small known distance d apart, connected in series so that the same current I flows in each, in opposite directions. The lower conductor is fixed; the upper one is one arm of a sensitive balance, so that the repulsive magnetic force lifts it. Measurement: small known masses are added to the upper conductor until it returns to its original position with the current flowing, so that the magnetic force equals the added weight, F = m g. Calculation: F = mu0 I^2 L/(2 pi d), so I = sqrt(2 pi d m g/(mu0 L)). Precaution: eliminate or allow for the earth's magnetic field and other stray fields (for example by orienting the conductors along the earth's horizontal field, or repeating with the current reversed), and keep d small compared with L so that the long-wire result applies.
s: Arrangement: two parallel conductors in series, one fixed and one on a balance
Measurement of force by balancing with a known weight, and I = sqrt(2 pi d m g/(mu0 L))
A valid precaution (earth's or stray fields, d much less than L)

concepts.name: Torque on a current loop and the magnetic dipole moment
concepts.description: The torque on a current loop in a uniform magnetic field, the magnetic moment m = N I A, stable and unstable equilibrium, and the current loop as a magnetic dipole with its far field.
concepts.idea: A current loop in a uniform magnetic field feels no net push, but it is twisted until its face is square-on to the field, just as a compass needle turns to line up with a field.
concepts.rule: A rectangular loop of sides a and b carrying current I in a uniform field B experiences no net force, but the equal and opposite forces I b B on two opposite arms form a couple of torque I A B sin(theta), where A = ab and theta is the angle between the field and the NORMAL to the loop. Defining the magnetic moment m = I A (m = N I A for N closely wound turns), directed along the normal given by the right-hand thumb rule, the torque is tau = m x B, with magnitude m B sin(theta); the unit of m is A m^2. The torque is zero when m is parallel to B (stable equilibrium) or antiparallel to B (unstable equilibrium), and greatest when the plane of the loop is parallel to the field. A planar current loop is equivalent to a magnetic dipole: far from a small loop (x much greater than R), the field on its axis is B = (mu0/4 pi) 2m/x^3 and in its plane B = (mu0/4 pi) m/x^3, the analogues of the electric dipole fields with mu0 replacing 1/epsilon0 and m replacing p. Unlike electric charges, magnetic monopoles are not known to exist.
concepts.example: A 100-turn circular coil of radius 10 cm carrying 3.2 A has m = N I A = 100 x 3.2 x 3.14 x 10^-2 = 10 A m^2; in a field of 2 T with m perpendicular to B the torque is m B = 20 N m.

questions.q: The SI unit of magnetic moment can be written as A m^n. The value of n is ____ (a whole number).
A planar coil of N closely wound turns, each of area A, carries a current I. The magnitude of its magnetic moment is
questions.a: N I A

questions.q: A rectangular loop carrying a steady current is placed in a uniform magnetic field. The net force on the loop is
questions.a: zero for every orientation of the loop
o: zero for every orientation of the loop
zero only when the plane of the loop is perpendicular to the field

questions.q: A rectangular loop ABCD carrying a current is placed with its plane parallel to a uniform magnetic field, the field being parallel to the arms AD and BC. Explain why the loop experiences no net force but does experience a torque.
questions.a: The arms AD and BC are parallel to the field, so the force on each is zero. The arms AB and CD are perpendicular to the field and carry current in opposite directions, so the forces on them, each of magnitude I b B (b being their length), are equal and opposite and the net force is zero. But these two forces do not act along the same line: they are separated by the width a of the loop and so form a couple, which gives a torque I a b B = I A B tending to rotate the loop.
s: Forces on the arms: zero on two, equal and opposite on the other two, so net force zero
The equal and opposite forces are not collinear, forming a couple of torque IAB

questions.q: A rectangular coil of 100 turns, each of area 0.02 m^2, carries a current of 2.5 A. It is free to rotate about an axis in its own plane, perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T, and its moment of inertia about this axis is 0.04 kg m^2. It is released from rest with its magnetic moment perpendicular to the field. Find (a) the magnetic moment of the coil, (b) the torque on it at the moment of release, and (c) its angular speed when its magnetic moment has turned to lie along the field.
questions.a: (a) m = N I A = 100 x 2.5 x 0.02 = 5 A m^2. (b) At release theta = 90 degrees, so torque = m B sin 90 = 5 x 0.4 = 2 N m. (c) Using (moment of inertia) x d(omega)/dt = m B sin(theta) and integrating as the angle between m and B falls from 90 degrees to 0, the work done by the torque is m B, so (1/2) x (moment of inertia) x omega^2 = m B. Hence omega = sqrt(2 m B/moment of inertia) = sqrt(2 x 5 x 0.4/0.04) = sqrt(100) = 10 rad/s.
s: (a) m = 5 A m^2
(b) Torque at release = 2 N m
(c) (1/2) x moment of inertia x omega^2 = mB, giving omega = 10 rad/s

questions.q: A current-carrying circular loop lies flat on a smooth horizontal table. Analyse whether a uniform magnetic field can be set up in such a direction that the loop spins about the vertical axis through its centre.
questions.a: No. The torque on the loop is m x B, which is always perpendicular to the magnetic moment m. For a loop lying in a horizontal plane, m (along the area vector) is vertical, so for any direction of B the torque is horizontal, lying in the plane of the loop. Turning the loop about the vertical axis would need a torque along the vertical direction, which a uniform field can never provide.
s: Torque m x B is perpendicular to m, and m is vertical for a horizontal loop
So the torque is always horizontal; rotation about the vertical axis is impossible

questions.q: For a small current loop of magnetic moment m, compare the magnetic field at a large distance x on its axis with the field at the same distance in its plane. Then set out the analogy with an electric dipole by stating which electric quantities correspond to m, to mu0 and to B, and state one fundamental difference between an electric dipole and a magnetic dipole.
questions.a: At a large distance x on the axis, B = (mu0/4 pi) 2m/x^3, and at the same distance in the plane of the loop, B = (mu0/4 pi) m/x^3; so the axial field is twice the field in the plane, and both fall off as 1/x^3. Analogy: these have the same form as the electric dipole fields 2p/(4 pi epsilon0 x^3) on the axis and p/(4 pi epsilon0 x^3) on the perpendicular bisector, with m corresponding to the electric dipole moment p, mu0 corresponding to 1/epsilon0, and B corresponding to E. Fundamental difference: an electric dipole is built from two elementary units, the electric charges (monopoles), whereas magnetic monopoles are not known to exist, so the magnetic dipole (current loop) is itself the most elementary magnetic element.
s: Axial field (mu0/4 pi) 2m/x^3 is twice the field in the plane (mu0/4 pi) m/x^3
Correspondence m with p, mu0 with 1/epsilon0, B with E
Difference: electric dipole made of charges; no magnetic monopoles

questions.q: A circular coil in a uniform magnetic field is replaced by a planar coil of irregular shape that has the same number of turns, carries the same current and encloses the same area, held at the same orientation. A student claims the torque on it will be different because its shape is different. Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. The torque on a planar current loop is m B sin(theta) with m = N I A, which depends only on the number of turns, the current, the enclosed area and the angle between the normal and the field, not on the shape of the loop. Since N, I, A, B and the orientation are unchanged, the torque is the same.
s: Torque = N I A B sin(theta) depends on area, not on shape
All these quantities are unchanged, so the torque is the same

questions.q: Design a coil (number of turns, dimensions and current) on which a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T exerts a maximum torque of 0.6 N m. Verify your design by calculation and state how the coil must be oriented for the torque to have this maximum value.
questions.a: Maximum torque = m B, so the magnetic moment needed is m = 0.6/0.5 = 1.2 A m^2, and N I A = 1.2 A m^2. One possible design: a rectangular coil of 100 turns, 8 cm x 5 cm (area 0.08 x 0.05 = 4 x 10^-3 m^2), carrying 3 A. Check: m = 100 x 3 x 4 x 10^-3 = 1.2 A m^2 and maximum torque = 1.2 x 0.5 = 0.6 N m. Orientation: the torque has this maximum value when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, that is, when the normal to the coil (the magnetic moment) is perpendicular to the field.
s: Required magnetic moment m = 1.2 A m^2 from torque = mB
A definite design with N I A = 1.2 A m^2, verified
Orientation: plane of the coil parallel to the field (m perpendicular to B)

concepts.name: The moving coil galvanometer and its conversion to an ammeter and a voltmeter
concepts.description: How a moving coil galvanometer turns current into a steady deflection, its current and voltage sensitivity, and how a shunt or a series resistance converts it into an ammeter or a voltmeter.
concepts.idea: A coil in a magnetic field twists in proportion to the current through it against a spring, so the angle of the pointer measures the current.
concepts.rule: A moving coil galvanometer has a coil of N turns and area A free to rotate in a uniform radial magnetic field B; a cylindrical soft iron core makes the field radial and increases its strength. Because the field is radial, sin(theta) = 1 and the magnetic torque is N I A B. A spring of torsional constant k gives a restoring torque k phi, so in equilibrium k phi = N I A B and the deflection is phi = (N A B/k) I. Current sensitivity is the deflection per unit current, phi/I = N A B/k; voltage sensitivity is the deflection per unit voltage, phi/V = (N A B/k)(1/R). Doubling the turns doubles the current sensitivity but also doubles the resistance, leaving the voltage sensitivity unchanged. To make an ammeter, a small shunt resistance rs is connected in parallel with the coil, so most of the current bypasses the coil and the instrument's resistance RG rs/(RG + rs) is small; an ammeter is connected in series. To make a voltmeter, a large resistance R is connected in series with the galvanometer, so that it draws very little current; a voltmeter is connected in parallel.
concepts.example: A 3.00 V cell in series with 3.00 ohm gives 1.00 A with an ideal ammeter, 3/63 = 0.048 A if a 60 ohm galvanometer is put in series, and 3/3.02 = 0.99 A once the galvanometer is shunted with 0.02 ohm.

questions.q: Give two reasons why a moving coil galvanometer cannot, as such, be used as an ammeter to measure the current in a circuit.
questions.a: (i) A galvanometer is a very sensitive device: it gives a full-scale deflection for a very small current, of the order of microamperes, so it cannot measure ordinary circuit currents. (ii) To measure a current the instrument must be connected in series, and since the galvanometer coil has a large resistance, putting it in series would change (reduce) the very current that is to be measured.

questions.q: A galvanometer of resistance 99 ohm gives a full-scale deflection for a current of 10 mA. Find the resistance that must be connected in parallel with it so that the instrument reads up to 1 A at full scale.
questions.a: At full scale 10 mA = 0.01 A flows through the galvanometer and the rest, 1 - 0.01 = 0.99 A, through the parallel (shunt) resistance. The two are in parallel, so they have the same potential difference: 0.01 x 99 = 0.99 x rs. Hence rs = 0.99/0.99 = 1 ohm.
s: Shunt carries 0.99 A with the same potential difference as the galvanometer (0.99 V)

questions.q: A cell of emf 2.00 V and negligible internal resistance is connected to a 4.00 ohm resistor. Find the current that flows when the current-measuring instrument connected in series is (a) a galvanometer of resistance 36.0 ohm and (b) an ideal ammeter of zero resistance. The galvanometer's large resistance in series reduces the current to one-tenth of its true value, which is why a galvanometer cannot be used as it is to measure the current.
s: (a) I = 0.05 A with the galvanometer in series
(b) I = 0.5 A with the ideal ammeter, and comment that the galvanometer changes the current

questions.q: Two moving coil meters M1 and M2 have springs of the same torsional constant. M1 has resistance 20 ohm, 50 turns, coil area 4 x 10^-3 m^2 and field 0.2 T. M2 has resistance 30 ohm, 100 turns, coil area 2 x 10^-3 m^2 and field 0.3 T. Find the ratio of (a) the current sensitivity and (b) the voltage sensitivity of M2 to that of M1.
questions.a: Current sensitivity = N A B/k. For M1: N A B = 50 x 4 x 10^-3 x 0.2 = 0.04. For M2: N A B = 100 x 2 x 10^-3 x 0.3 = 0.06. With the same k, (a) the ratio of current sensitivities M2 : M1 = 0.06/0.04 = 1.5. Voltage sensitivity = N A B/(k R). (b) Ratio M2 : M1 = (0.06/30)/(0.04/20) = 0.002/0.002 = 1. So M2 is 1.5 times as sensitive to current but the two have equal voltage sensitivity.
s: N A B evaluated: 0.04 for M1 and 0.06 for M2
(a) Current sensitivity ratio 1.5
(b) Voltage sensitivity ratio 1, using division by resistance

questions.q: Two 1000 ohm resistors are connected in series across a 6 V battery of negligible internal resistance. A voltmeter of resistance 1000 ohm is connected across one of the resistors. Find the voltmeter reading, compare it with the voltage across that resistor before the voltmeter was connected, and explain the difference.
questions.a: Before the voltmeter is connected, the 6 V divides equally and each resistor has 3 V across it. With the voltmeter connected, the 1000 ohm voltmeter in parallel with one 1000 ohm resistor makes 500 ohm; the total is 500 + 1000 = 1500 ohm, the current is 6/1500 = 0.004 A and the voltmeter reads 0.004 x 500 = 2 V. The reading is lower than 3 V because the voltmeter's resistance is not large compared with the resistor, so it draws an appreciable current and disturbs the circuit; a voltmeter should have a very large resistance.
s: Reading 2 V (parallel combination 500 ohm, current 0.004 A)
True value 3 V; voltmeter draws current because its resistance is not large enough

questions.q: A galvanometer has a resistance of 90 ohm and gives a full-scale deflection for 10 mA. (a) Find the parallel resistance needed to convert it into an ammeter of range 0 to 100 mA. (b) Find the series resistance needed to convert it into a voltmeter of range 0 to 10 V. (c) Find the resistance of each finished instrument and comment on why these values suit the way each instrument is connected.
questions.a: (a) At full scale the galvanometer carries 10 mA and the shunt 90 mA, with the same potential difference 0.010 x 90 = 0.9 V, so rs = 0.9/0.090 = 10 ohm. (b) At full scale 10 mA must flow when 10 V is applied, so the total resistance is 10/0.010 = 1000 ohm and the series resistance is 1000 - 90 = 910 ohm. (c) Ammeter resistance = (90 x 10)/(90 + 10) = 9 ohm, lower than the galvanometer's: an ammeter goes in series, so a low resistance changes the circuit current little. Voltmeter resistance = 1000 ohm, much higher than the galvanometer's: a voltmeter goes in parallel, so a high resistance makes it draw little current.
s: (a) Shunt = 10 ohm
(b) Series resistance = 910 ohm
(c) Ammeter 9 ohm (low, used in series); voltmeter 1000 ohm (high, used in parallel)

questions.q: To measure the current through a resistor, a student connects an ammeter in parallel with the resistor instead of in series. Evaluate this method.
questions.a: The method is wrong. An ammeter must be in series so that the current to be measured passes through it. An ammeter has a very small resistance (a galvanometer with a small shunt), so connected in parallel it offers an easy path: most of the current bypasses the resistor and flows through the ammeter, the total current in the circuit rises sharply, and the reading is not the current that was flowing through the resistor (and the large current may damage the meter).
s: Ammeter must be in series to carry the current being measured
In parallel its small resistance diverts most of the current, giving a wrong (large) reading

questions.q: You are given a galvanometer of resistance 48 ohm that gives a full-scale deflection for 2 mA. Design, with calculations, (a) an ammeter of range 0 to 50 mA and (b) a voltmeter of range 0 to 5 V based on it, stating the value of the resistance needed in each case and how it is connected, and verify each design.
questions.a: (a) Ammeter: connect a shunt in parallel with the galvanometer. At full scale the galvanometer carries 2 mA and the shunt 48 mA, with the same potential difference 0.002 x 48 = 0.096 V, so rs = 0.096/0.048 = 2 ohm. Check: with 50 mA entering, the 2 ohm shunt takes 48 mA and the 48 ohm coil takes 2 mA, which is full scale. (b) Voltmeter: connect a large resistance R in series. At full scale 2 mA flows with 5 V across the instrument, so the total resistance is 5/0.002 = 2500 ohm and R = 2500 - 48 = 2452 ohm. Check: 0.002 x (2452 + 48) = 5 V.
s: (a) Shunt of 2 ohm in parallel
(b) Series resistance of 2452 ohm
Each design verified by calculation
